# Maternal obesity, gestational weight gain and offspring asthma and atopy

**Authors:** Kristen J. Polinski; Griffith A. Bell; Mai-Han Trinh; Rajeshwari Sundaram; Pauline Mendola; Sonia L. Robinson; Erin M. Bell; Temilayo Adeyeye; Tzu-Chun Lin; Edwina H. Yeung

**Affiliations:** 1Division of Population Health Research, Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD; | 2Ariadne Labs, Boston, MA; | 3Departments of Health Policy and Management, and of Epidemiology, Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA; | 4Department of Epidemiology and Environmental Health, University at Buffalo, State University of New York, Buffalo, NY; | 5Department of Environmental Health Sciences, University at Albany, State University of New York, Albany, NY; | 6Glotech Inc., Rockville, MD

## Abstract

Maternal obesity may affect offspring asthma and atopic disease risk by altering fetal immune system development. However, few studies examine gestational weight gain (GWG).

Examine relationships between maternal body mass index (BMI), GWG, and persistent wheeze, eczema, allergy, and asthma risk in offspring through middle childhood.

A total of 5939 children from Upstate KIDS, a population-based longitudinal cohort of children born in upstate New York (2008–2019) were included in analysis. Persistent wheeze or asthma, eczema, and allergy were maternally reported at multiple study timepoints throughout early and middle childhood. Poisson regression models with robust standard errors were used to estimate adjusted risk ratios (aRR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for offspring atopic outcomes by maternal pre-pregnancy BMI and GWG.

Pre-pregnancy BMI was associated with increased risk of persistent wheeze by 3 years of age even after adjustments for maternal atopy (class I obesity: aRR 1.58, 95% CI: 1.13, 2.20; class II/III obesity: aRR 1.69, 95% CI: 1.22, 2.35). Associations with reported asthma in middle childhood did not reach statistical significance. Further, no associations were found between prepregnancy BMI and atopic outcomes in either early or middle childhood. GWG was not associated with higher risk of early childhood persistent wheeze or middle childhood asthma.

Maternal pre-pregnancy BMI was associated with increased risk of offspring wheeze, while excessive GWG was generally not associated with childhood asthma/atopy.

## Introduction

Prevalence of maternal obesity, high gestational weight gain (GWG) and atopic disease have increased over the past several decades.1–3 Approximately 30% of women of reproductive age in the United States are obese, and a growing body of research has documented numerous adverse health outcomes in the offspring of women with obesity.1 Similarly, 47.2% and 20.9% of women had excessive or inadequate GWG, respectively based on the Institute of Medicine guidelines (IoM, recently renamed the National Academies of Medicine) guidelines.4,5 Obesity is widely considered a state of low-grade chronic inflammation, marked by higher levels of cytokines and C-reactive protein. In line with the developmental origins of health and disease hypothesis, prenatal exposures to maternal obesity may have implications for development of the immune system of the offspring in utero.6

Concurrently, there is concerning evidence of increasing global prevalence of atopic diseases that may be related to socioeconomic determinants of health like obesity.2,7,8 Atopic diseases are IgE mediated conditions such as atopic dermatitis/eczema, food allergy and allergic asthma. Prevalence of food allergy has increased up to 10% in recent years and the estimated prevalence of atopic dermatitis among U.S. children is 13%.9,10 Additionally asthma is one of the most common chronic conditions among children and though asthma is comprised of multiple clinical phenotypes, childhood-onset asthma typically fits in to the allergic phenotype.11 Such allergic diseases are rarely fatal, but they can have substantial impact on quality of life and may increase incidence of more serious conditions in adulthood.6,12 While atopic diseases may manifest symptoms as a result of sensitization to environmental risk factors, research has shown that perinatal exposures may increase susceptibility to sensitization and progression of the “atopic march.”.7,13

Meta-analyses have reported fairly consistent evidence for increased risks of childhood asthma/wheeze associated with pre-pregnancy obesity.14–16 Though fewer studies have examined the effects of GWG on other non-asthma outcomes. For instance, a recent a meta-analysis explored associations of body mass index (BMI) and GWG with atopic dermatitis outcomes in offspring, in which high or excessive GWG was associated with an increased risk.17 However, this finding was based on only 2 studies examining GWG exposure in that meta-analysis and more recent findings found no associations between GWG and atopic dermatitis.18,19 If GWG places offspring at increased risk of atopic disease, modifying weight gain has the potential to decrease morbidity and GWG can be used to identify and monitor offspring at high risk. Therefore, we examined the associations of pre-pregnancy BMI and GWG on both asthma and other atopic outcomes, including eczema/atopic dermatitis, through middle childhood in a prospective cohort study.

## Methods

### Study Population

Our study used data on maternal weight, lifestyle factors and allergic disease in offspring collected in the Upstate KIDS Study, a large, population-based longitudinal cohort study of 5,034 pregnancies and 6,171 offspring born in New York State (excluding New York City). Details of the sampling framework and recruitment procedures can be found elsewhere.20 Briefly, participants were recruited using the New York State livebirth registry to identify eligible children born between 2008 and 2010. All children conceived using fertility treatments as recorded on birth certificates were invited to participate in the study, as were all children of multiple births regardless of conception method. Children not conceived using fertility treatments were frequency matched to area of residence of those who were conceived using treatments at a 3:1 ratio. Follow-up of this cohort continued until 2019. The New York State Department of Health and the University at Albany Institutional Review Boards (IRB) approved the study, serving as the IRB designated by the National Institutes of Health under a reliance agreement. Parents provided written informed consent.

### Measurements

#### Maternal obesity and gestational weight gain

Maternal pre-pregnancy BMI was calculated using pre-pregnancy weight and height as provided in the birth certificate. If data were missing, maternal questionnaire data from 4 months postpartum were used. We examined BMI categorically as underweight (<18.5 kg/m2), normal weight (18.5–24.9 kg/m2), overweight (25–29.9 kg/m2), obese class I (30–34.9 kg/m2) or obese class II/III (≥35 kg/m2). Gestational weight gain was self-reported on maternal questionnaires. Categories of gestational weight gain were defined using the 2009 IoM guidelines.5 Adequate weight gain for singleton pregnancies was defined as 28–40, 25–35, 15–25, and 11–20 pounds total gestational weight gain for underweight, normal weight, overweight, or obese women, respectively. GWG guidelines of adequate weight gain for women with twin gestations were defined as 37–54, 31–50 and 25–42 pounds for women with of normal weight, overweight or obesity, respectively. GWG above or below these guidelines was categorized as excessive or inadequate.

#### Atopy

Data on infant wheeze, eczema/atopic dermatitis, and allergies were captured via maternal report on study questionnaires completed in early childhood. Persistent wheeze was defined as any two reports of wheeze at 4, 8, 12, 18, 24, 30, or 36 months of age. Eczema/atopic dermatitis was defined as any maternal report of physician-diagnosed eczema or atopic dermatitis at 8, 12, 18, 24, 30, or 36 months of age. Mothers were also asked to report if their toddler had a physician-diagnosed allergy to food, medicine, dust, animals, pollen, or ragweed at 8, 12, 18, 24, 30, or 36 months of age. For analysis of early childhood outcomes, we examined any atopy, as defined by any reported allergy, eczema/atopic dermatitis, or food allergy by 36 months age.

Middle childhood outcomes of asthma, eczema/atopic dermatitis and allergies were examined at approximately 7, 8, or 9 years of age when mothers completed questionnaires annually between 2016 – 2019. In middle childhood, asthma was defined as any maternal report of current physician-diagnosed asthma or prescription of asthma medication/inhaler in the past year. Eczema was defined as any report of physician-diagnosed eczema. Lastly, allergies were defined as any report of seeing a physician for allergy or use of allergy medication in the past year.

### Covariates

Maternal age at delivery, race/ethnicity, educational level, health insurance status data, and offspring birthweight and gestational age were collected from the birth certificate. Maternal atopy (defined by history of asthma, eczema, or allergy to food or pollen), marital status and maternal smoking habits were reported by mothers at 4 months postpartum. Gestational diabetes was based on indication in vital statistics records, discharge diagnoses derived from the Statewide Planning and Research Cooperative System (SPARCS), or maternal self-report at 4 months postpartum.

### Statistical analyses

We calculated descriptive statistics to examine distributions of the demographic and biological characteristics of participants by pre-pregnancy BMI categories and GWG categories. These comparisons were made at the family level (n=4,912) to avoid double counting information from families with twins. We used Poisson regression models with robust standard errors to estimate the relative risk (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the association between pre-pregnancy BMI, GWG, and atopic outcomes in unadjusted and multivariable adjusted models. Models included a random effect to account for the dependence between twins of the same family and were adjusted for maternal age, race/ethnicity, education, marital status, smoking during pregnancy, private health insurance, maternal history of atopy and plurality based on a priori mapping of causal relationships between exposures and outcomes using a directed acyclic graph. Models examining GWG as an exposure were additionally adjusted for maternal prepregnancy BMI and gestational age.

Because infants conceived by fertility treatment and twins were oversampled in this study, we used sampling weights in each model to account for this study design feature.20 To account for missing outcome data, we used inverse probability weighting. Sampling and inverse probability treatment weights were multiplied and then trimmed at the 95th percentile for analyses. To account for missing covariate data, 50 datasets were created using multiple imputation by chained equations.

Sensitivity analyses were performed. First, we used International Classification of Diseases 9th Revision (ICD-9) codes to identify early childhood asthma and allergy related conditions as registered in the SPARCS. SPARCS is a longitudinal inpatient and outpatient hospital discharge data system from the state of New York and would likely reflect the more severe cases of asthma or allergy. The ICD-9 codes for asthma and allergy related conditions are provided in the eTable 1. We conducted a survival analysis to assess if the time-to asthma or allergy based on the first reported ICD-9 code differs by categories of maternal pre-pregnancy BMI and GWG. The time scale was the child’s age in months as reported in SPARCS and participants were right censored at the end of the SPARCS linkage (age 40 months). We obtained Kaplan-Meier curves and log-rank p-values. Second, we examined associations of GWG with early and middle childhood atopic outcomes stratified by plurality status as previous literature suggests twins may be at an increased risk of early life wheeze or asthma.

Analyses were conducted using SAS 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC, U.S.A.).

## Results

Prepregnancy BMI and GWG differed by maternal age, education, marital status, smoking during pregnancy, insurance status, and gestational diabetes (Table 1). Prepregnancy BMI was also associated with maternal atopy and GWG was further associated with plurality and gestational age. By age 3 years, 10.8% of toddlers were reported to have persistent wheeze, 39.2% any atopy, 28.2% eczema/atopic dermatitis, and 10.2% any food allergy. The majority of infants with persistent wheeze had 1 to 2 reported wheeze attacks at each assessment. In SPARCS, 145 (3.8%) had at least one ICD-9 code consistent with an asthma-related condition and 34 (0.9%) had at least one ICD-9 code consistent with any allergy-related condition through 40 months of follow-up. By middle childhood, 16.5% of children had current asthma (physician diagnosis or medication in past year), 10.4% eczema, 16.7% with physician diagnosed allergies in past year, and 14.2% allergy medication prescribed in past year.

Table 2 presents the associations of pre-pregnancy BMI categories and atopy outcomes in early and middle childhood. We observed an increased risk of persistent wheeze among offspring of mothers with class I obesity (aRR: 1.45; 95% CI: 1.03, 2.03) and class II/III obesity (aRR: 1.51; 95% CI: 1.08, 2.11) as compared to normal weight prior to pregnancy. A borderline association for maternal class II/III obesity (aRR: 0.81; 95% CI: 0.66, 1.00) but not class I obesity (aRR: 1.03; 95% CI: 0.87, 1.22) was associated with decreased risk of eczema/atopic dermatitis in early childhood. No significant effects were observed with food allergy or atopy overall in early childhood. By middle childhood, we found no significant associations with asthma or eczema in the adjusted models. Pre-pregnancy BMI was positively associated with reported allergy at 7 to 9 years, but not use of allergy medication use. Children of women with overweight pre-pregnancy BMI were more likely to have reported allergy than children of women with normal pre-pregnancy BMI (aRR: 1.72; 95% CI: 1.18, 2.51). A similar trend was observed among children of women with class I or class II/III obesity though these associations did not reach statistical significance.

Table 3 presents the associations of GWG based on IOM guidelines and atopy outcomes in early and middle childhood; in which, we found no associations with persistent wheeze, asthma, or eczema. In analyses examining early childhood allergies to foods only, offspring of women with GWG below IoM guidelines had a decreased risk of developing food allergies by 36 months compared to offspring of women with GWG within the guidelines (aRR 0.64; 95% CI: 0.44, 0.94). Notably, after a Bonferroni p-value adjustment for multiple comparisons, this association did not reach statistical significance. In the sensitivity analysis, in which we stratified by plurality status, we found that this association held in singletons (RR: 0.63; 0.42, 0.95), but was limited in precision in the twins (RR: 0.76; 95% CI: 0.49, 1.19). No other significant differences in outcomes by GWG or pre-pregnancy BMI were found when repeating our analysis in singletons (eTable 2) and twins (eTable 3) separately.

Lastly, in our sensitivity analysis reflecting the more severe cases of early childhood asthma or allergy in our cohort, we did not find statistically significant associations with pre-pregnancy BMI and any severe allergy requiring in/out-patient hospital care (log-rank p-value 0.38; eFigure 1) or with asthma requiring in/out-patient care (log-rank p-value 0.70; eFigure 2). Nor did we find associations with GWG and severe allergy episode (log-rank p-value 0.14; eFigure 3) or asthma-related ICD-9 codes (log-rank p-value 0.53; eFigure 4).

## Discussion

In our population-based, longitudinal cohort, we found evidence that pre-pregnancy obesity was associated with increased risks of persistent wheeze by 3 years of age but not asthma in middle childhood nor hospital visits due to asthma. Pre-pregnancy overweight may have a positive but lesser effect on persistent wheeze. A higher pre-pregnancy BMI was also consistent with elevated maternal report of offspring allergy in middle childhood but was not associated with early childhood allergy. GWG was generally not associated with offspring persistent wheeze or asthma. We did observe that children born to mothers with inadequate GWG had a modest decreased risk of food related allergies in early childhood, but this finding did not withstand adjustment for multiple testing by Bonferroni correction (p<0.0125) and should be interpreted cautiously. Neither inadequate nor excessive weight gain were associated with middle childhood atopy outcomes.

Our findings regarding a modest elevated risk of persistent wheeze among children of women with higher pre-pregnancy BMI, particularly BMI ≥ 30, is consistent with previous studies, including a recent meta-analysis of 22 studies by Liu et al. that examined wheeze and/or asthma outcomes16,18,21–33, though our findings by middle childhood suggest no significant positive associations between pre-pregnancy BMI and asthma after adjustment for potential confounders. Fewer studies have examined GWG and offspring wheeze/asthma and Liu et. al. identified differences in findings based on how GWG was defined.16 High or low GWG categories (not based on IoM recommendations) were positively associated with childhood asthma/wheeze. However, when GWG was assessed according to IoM recommendations (like our study), Liu et. al. found a non-significant inverse association between excessive GWG and asthma/wheeze based on three studies (average ages were 1, 4 and 6).16,29,32,34 Further, two recent analyses by Wei et al. and Srugo et al. also reported no significant associations between GWG according to IoM guidelines and asthma/wheeze outcomes.18,19 These findings are consistent with our findings of GWG and persistent wheeze or asthma in early and middle childhood.

Studies examining the associations of atopic diseases, such as eczema or food allergy, with pre-pregnancy BMI or GWG have had mixed results.17–19,24,28,33 A meta-analysis by Chen et al., reported pre-pregnancy overweight and obesity was protective in the development of atopic dermatitis based on 6 – 7 studies (effect sizes ranging from 0.80 to 1.09 for children 3 – 17 years).17 Additionally, Goudarzi et al. observed a protective effect of maternal BMI on eczema at age 7 years within a Japanese birth cohort.28 We similarly noted eczema effect sizes of 0.81 and 0.93 in the class II/III obesity adjusted models for early and middle childhood, respectively. In this same meta-analysis, Chen et al., determined that high or excessive GWG was associated with an increased risk of atopic dermatitis; whereas, low or inadequate GWG was associated with a decreased risk based only on 2 – 3 studies.17,23,33,35 Two more recent studies reported no associations between GWG and atopic dermatitis outcomes, similar to our findings in early and middle childhood.18,19 Few studies have examined food allergy outcomes. Like Kumar et. al., we found no association of food allergy with pre-pregnancy BMI.24 Yet, in a recent cross-sectional study of over eight thousand children, pre-pregnancy overweight or obesity was associated with an increased likelihood of food allergy in offspring age 3 to 14 years.33 That same study also found that children born to mothers with inadequate GWG based on IoM guidelines were less likely to have food allergy which is consistent with the direction of our results. Though after stratifying for BMI, the association did not remain.33

Several biological pathways explaining the relationship between maternal weight and offspring atopy have been hypothesized.36,37 One pathway may involve the downstream impact of pre-pregnancy obesity on exposure to inflammation, which in turn may have implications for the offspring microbiome.6,38–41 Nutrients are transported to the fetus through the placenta, which may play an important role in immune system development. Increased levels of lipids in the placentas of women with obesity may cause increases in macrophages and inflammatory factors.6 Studies of infants born to women with obesity have also observed elevated levels of numerous inflammatory cytokines, such as leptin and TNF-α in their cord blood, which is also associated with wheeze in children.30 In Upstate KIDS, we reported no associations between maternal obesity or GWG with IgE concentrations – through which atopic reactions can be mediated – in newborn dried blood spots, but levels of inflammatory markers were associated with having BMI ≥ 35.42 During the birth process, newborn immunoglobulins and inflammatory markers can have high variability in response to birth stress, potentially making associations with pre-pregnancy BMI or GWG difficult to detect.43 Evidence from other studies of maternal obesity and allergic sensitization is mixed, with a report of maternal obesity not associated with allergic sensitization in offspring, while another study reports an association between maternal obesity and decreased cord blood IgE.22,24 Maternal obesity can also increase the offspring’s own risk of obesity, which is in turn a risk factor for wheezing and asthma.30 Further, research into the microbiomes of obese mothers and their offspring also suggests that changes in gut microbiome may play a role in infant immune development and risk of allergy and atopic disease.30,44 Taken together, these findings suggest that pre-pregnancy weight and GWG may be related to allergic disease through complex, multifactorial pathways. Better characterization of this relationship will also provide more complete scientific evidence for future GWG guideline development.

The strengths of this study include the longitudinal design and follow-up through middle childhood. Our study has several limitations. First, the study was not designed with the intent to clinically validate diagnoses of atopic disease. Outcome data were based on maternal self-report of physician’s diagnoses which may be inaccurate. Misclassification of this type would likely add non-differential measurement error in the outcome, which might limit our ability to detect an association. Second, GWG is only measured across the entirety of the pregnancy, with no trimester-specific measurements available, though gestational age was accounted for in the models. Third, as this was an observational study, residual confounding cannot be ruled out; however, we were able to measure and adjust for numerous lifestyle and demographic characteristics measured in the baseline questionnaire (before reports of atopy) that were confirmed in subsequent follow-up questionnaires. Finally, the associations presented do not imply causality and more studies are needed to help establish a causal relationship between prepregnancy BMI, gestational weight gain and risk of atopy in the offspring.

## Conclusion

Reports of pre-pregnancy obesity, high GWG, and allergic disease have increased over the past 20 years. In our population-based, longitudinal birth cohort study, we found that children of mothers with higher BMIs had higher risk of persistent wheeze in early childhood. The role of gestational weight gain remains unclear and require potentially more information on timing of weight gain. Future studies should explore these relationships in different settings with physician validated diagnosis of atopy to replicate these findings.
